title: [Full Workshop] Vibe Coding at Scale: Customizing AI Assistants for Enterprise Environments
talk_summary: A VS Code team member demos GitHub Copilot's agent mode across three 'vibe coding' maturity stages (yolo, structured, spectrum), emphasizing reusable instructions, scoped custom modes, prompt files, and MCP tool-set curation.

takeaways.what_they_do: They define named tool sets and bind specific tools to specific modes/prompts so the model isn't choosing among an exploding MCP tool list; they also let users explicitly mention the exact tool to invoke.
takeaways.evidence_quote: in your modes boil down the tools to what you actually need. So reducing the tools manually

takeaways.technique: Scoped instruction files with glob front-matter
takeaways.what_they_do: Beyond one monolithic instructions file, they support per-path instruction files with front-matter globs so rules apply only when matching files are in context; they also warn monolith files get unwieldy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they start to be scoped with a glob pattern and then right now they're limited to being applied

takeaways.technique: Reusable prompt files as shared team artifacts
takeaways.what_they_do: They promote ad-hoc Slack-copied prompts into versioned prompt files invocable via slash command, so a champion's one-shotting prompt is reused by everyone; prompts are task-oriented vs instructions being how-to.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can finally put these prompts into a place where they can just be used by everybody

takeaways.technique: Spec → plan → implement as separate modes
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue for spending more time up front: write the spec, then the implementation plan, then implement, using separate modes; also use AI as a critic that pokes holes in the spec before coding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: write the spec write the plan and then implement. So you would even have three modes if you do it correctly

takeaways.technique: Custom modes with constrained tools and confirmation gates
takeaways.what_they_do: Custom agent modes are markdown-defined, can restrict which tools they use, and can be told to pause for user confirmation at defined points (e.g. after red tests before implementation).
takeaways.evidence_quote: in a mode you can say which tools it's supposed to use

takeaways.technique: TDD mode: red tests then confirm then implement
takeaways.what_they_do: A custom mode enforces test-first: understand problem, write failing tests, get confirmation, then implement and keep running tests; they note it only works if the test tooling is actually wired up.
takeaways.evidence_quote: write tests first and only after tests are done maybe get confirmation from the user to then write the implementation
